articles.title: Saudi strike kills ’11 civilians’ in Yemen’s Taiz: Houthi media
articles.summary: Hostilities between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed coalition continue to push Yemen into a humanitarian crisis.
articles.body:
Saudi air strikes have killed 11 civilians in Yemen’s Taiz governorate, according to news media affiliated with the Houthi armed group.

The attack reported on Friday hit the city of al-Turbah, located south of the provincial capital, Taiz.

The alleged strike comes as hostilities in Yemen continue between the Iran-backed rebel Houthi group and government forces backed by Saudi Arabia.

A local source said that a residential building was struck and that “most” of the victims were children, according to the media report.

Rescue teams retrieved eight bodies from the site, the report said. Three people remain missing beneath the rubble.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify the reports. The Saudi Arabia-led coalition supporting the internationally-recognised Yemen government did not immediately comment.

The coalition said later on Friday that it had destroyed a drone launched by the Houthis toward Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh region.

Yemen has been racked by violence since the Iran-backed Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and other parts of the country in 2014, prompting Saudi Arabia to lead a military coalition in support of the internationally recognised government in March 2015.

Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis resumed in July, as the United States’ war on Iran escalated hostilities and the collapse of a 2022 ceasefire.

Some 13,343 people have been killed or injured since August, according to the World Health Organization, while the country is sliding into a humanitarian crisis.

The Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme said on Friday that Yemen is among conflict hotspots that face severe food insecurity.

The Norwegian Refugee Council warned this week that the renewed fighting has displaced thousands and piled pressure onto dangerously underfunded aid efforts.

Aid from the US, Germany and others has shrunk considerably in recent years, the nongovernmental organisation noted, saying it has received only 12 percent of funding for emergency shelter support in Yemen so far this year.

“Fighting has again displaced entire communities, while disrupted supply routes have driven up food and fuel prices,” NRC Secretary-General Jan Egeland said, warning that families across Yemen are being pushed deeper into need.

“All parties to the conflict bear responsibility for the vast scale of harm here,” Egeland stated.

Calling for better humanitarian access and civilian protection, he demanded that “the powerful countries backing the armed actors must commit to making this a reality”.

articles.body: CHENNAI: Kallakurichi TVK MLA C Arul Vignesh was arrested on Friday, four days after a woman officer lodged a formal sexual harassment complaint against the ruling party legislator. The arrest brought curtains down on the controversy over the delayed action against the MLA despite social and bureaucratic outrage.On Friday evening, Tamil Nadu director-general of police’s office issued a statement saying that the woman officer lodged a complaint at Kallakurichi all-women police station on Nov 23. Police registered a case under Section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Prohibition of Harassment of Women Act and four provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).The charges included Section 75(1)(i) read with Section 75(2), relating to unwelcome physical contact and advances; Section 75(1)(iv) read with Section 75(3), concerning sexually coloured remarks; Section 78(2), relating to stalking; and Section 132, concerning assault or criminal force against a public servant to deter the discharge of official duty.The local police initially investigated the complaint. Following an order by Madras high court on Nov 24, Tirupur district superintendent of police Shristi Singh took over the investigation under the supervision of inspector-general of police N Kamini.The investigating officer questioned the complainant and other witnesses as part of the probe. Police served a summons on Arul Vignesh at his residence in Kallakurichi on Nov 25.Sources said the decision to arrest Arul Vignesh was taken at a high-level meeting held by chief minister C Joseph Vijay at his official Pamini Illam residence on Greenways Road on Friday evening. Chief secretary Sai Kumar, DGP Mahesh Kumar Aggarwal, inspector-general of state intelligence) Asra Garg and other senior officials participated in the meeting. Minutes after the meeting, instructions were passed on to apprehend the Arul Vignesh in the sexual harassment case.A police team led by a deputy superintendent of police and inspector P Bhuvaneshwari of the all-women police station reached the MLA’s residence around 6.15pm with an arrest warrant issued by Kallakurichi magistrate court. The team showed him the warrant before taking him into custody. They had accused the state govt of delaying action.Friday’s DGP office statement also said that the cybercrime wing of the state police had removed at least 201 social media posts relating to the incident. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress on Friday termed the NCP (SP)'s decision to back the Centre's delimitation Bill \"unfortunate\", saying that such a decision should have
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress on Friday termed the NCP (SP)'s decision to back the Centre's delimitation Bill "unfortunate", saying that such a decision should have been taken at the INDIA bloc meeting.Reacting to NCP (SP) leader Jitendra Awhad's statement, Maharashtra Congress spokesperson Sachin Sawant expressed surprise at the decision and said that Sharad Pawar's political journey had been associated with secular and democratic values.Asserting the importance of opposition unity and collective decision-making, Sawant told news agency PTI, "Whether the NCP (SP) decision was taken under pressure or was driven by political calculations will become clear with time."Sawant also said that the government's intention behind the Bill was not genuine and that it was aimed at further tightening its grip on power. He also questioned the rationale behind the proposed exercise in the absence of a fresh Census."This is called gerrymandering. articles.title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
articles.summary: Stormy weather in New York City prompted organisers to push back the Macy's parade by two days - leaving some musicians stuck.
articles.body:
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.

"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.

Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.

Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.

On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.

The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.

The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.

Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather

Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving

Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band.

"My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he said.

"Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?"

The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of New York City during the holidays.

There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.

Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal.

"The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich said, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses.

He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend".

"We have a lot to be thankful for this Thanksgiving."

Meanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.

Speaking to the BBC earlier on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.

The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.

"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional for our students," Badua said.

But the musicians sprang into action quickly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".

The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.

Badua was hopeful his group would have the same experience he had when he first performed at the parade in 2003, as student drum major.

"The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great."

Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it was trying to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.

"Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Professor Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.

While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain brought by the storm to eastern areas of the US.

Hundreds of thousands of homes were without power in the storm's aftermath Friday, and coastal areas had flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.

articles.title: Serbia’s student-led movement nominates chemistry professor for presidency
articles.summary: Radomir Saicic, who teaches at Belgrade University, was among the first university professors to join the movement.
articles.body:
Serbia’s student-backed movement, which won an October election after rallying against corruption, has named university professor Radomir Saicic as its presidential candidate in next month’s polls.

Saicic, who teaches chemistry at Belgrade University, is a member of the newly elected parliament as a representative of the Student List, which won 140 seats in the 250-member parliament.

The role is largely ceremonial, but the president is responsible for nominating prime ministers and serves as commander-in-chief of the armed forces.

The December 27 presidential vote comes after Aleksandar Vucic – who dominated Serbian politics for 14 years – cut short his second presidential term to run for prime minister but was soundly defeated by the student-led movement in the parliamentary ballot.

Speaking at a televised news conference in Belgrade on Friday, Saicic said the movement must now prioritise strengthening the rule of law and fighting corruption.

“Now we have the opportunity to turn the freedom we fought for into lasting change,” he said.

“The assembly, the government and the courts must once again earn the trust of the people. The same applies to the institution of the president.”

Saicic pledged a “sovereign Serbia in which the constitution will be respected and in which every citizen will be able to live with dignity”.

Saicic, 65, is also a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts, and was among the first university professors to join the student-led protest movement that emerged in 2024.

He said he was proud that students trusted him enough to put him forward as a presidential candidate, adding that “the last decade was marred by the crumbling of the rule of law, corruption and hate speech”.

“The outgoing regime is still trying to disintegrate our state,” he said. “In order to prevent this, we need to restore the institutions.”

Vucic, now an opposition member of parliament, has repeatedly suggested his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) might sit out the election, but a final decision is expected in mid-December.

Vucic himself is barred from running again as the constitution limits presidents to two terms.

The parliamentary and presidential elections followed nearly two years of protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people.

The disaster at the recently renovated station, widely blamed on corruption, triggered Serbia’s largest protests since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.

The movement’s initial demand for a transparent investigation evolved into calls for snap elections, which Vucic eventually announced after nearly two years of resistance.

articles.title: Paul Mackenzie: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
articles.summary: Paul Mackenzie is found guilty of killing his followers, weeks after being jailed for the mass murder of children.
articles.body:
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.

Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.

Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.

Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.

Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.

The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.

Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.

The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.

"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.

The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".

Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.

Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.

The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.

Earlier this week, Mackenzie was also convicted of:

assault causing actual bodily harm and five counts of cruelty to a child

facilitating the commission of a terrorist act

being in possession of an article connected with an offence under Kenya's Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2012.

Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders

Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.

A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.

His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".

After the main church shut down in 2019, Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest.

"We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," said survivor Peter Shukrani, who was rescued after falling ill.

When the shallow graves were discovered, local men were hired for the horrifying task of exhuming the remains.

"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."

"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."

Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".

Post-mortem records showed many of the victims had died of starvation while the remains of others were mostly skeletal, making the establishment of their cause of death impossible.

Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he had lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.

"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court last month.

"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest. I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."

The deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.

The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

articles.title: Trump backs Iraqi PM’s oil smuggling crackdown
articles.summary: Baghdad closes border crossings as Kurdish authorities warn of constitutional violations and call for meeting.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has backed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s drive to stop oil smuggling and assert state authority, moves that have put Baghdad in direct confrontation with Kurdish authorities and Iran-aligned militias.

Trump said in a Truth Social post on Friday that Washington supports al-Zaidi’s efforts to “stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state”.

He said the United States wants a “united, prosperous, and strong Iraq that makes its own political decisions”. The endorsement comes as al-Zaidi, who has steered Iraq closer to Washington, risks antagonising both the Kurds and Iran, Agence France-Presse reported.

Haider al-Aboudi told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that Baghdad considers crude exports bypassing state marketer SOMO to be smuggling, since the proceeds do not reach the treasury. He said Iraq lost an estimated $100bn to smuggling through northern Iraq’s Kurdish region between 2008 and 2025.

Reuters said it was unclear how the government calculated the figure.

On Tuesday, al-Zaidi moved to place the Kurdish region’s border crossings and several oil fields under federal control, AFP reported. Iraq closed two crossings in the region on Thursday, one with Syria and one with Iran. Iraq’s highest court ruled on Wednesday that Baghdad can deploy federal forces along all international borders, including those of the Kurdish region of northern Iraq.

Oil Minister Basim Mohammed said: “The oilfields in the region and Basra belong to all Iraqis and remain under the Iraqi flag.” INA reported that he said Iraq would not be lenient towards “any drop of oil exported outside legal contexts”.

Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) spokesman Peshawa Hawramani said the region does not want clashes with Baghdad, but sees the central government’s actions as aimed at restricting the semi-autonomous region and violating its constitutional rights.

“We are not in favour of clashes and disagreement, but that does not mean we accept the violation of Kurdistan’s rights guaranteed by the constitution,” he said.

The Kurdish government on Wednesday rejected the “military language and threats” in a statement from the Iraqi military spokesman, Reuters reported. It said it was working with federal authorities to combat corruption. Thousands of Kurds protested the decision on Thursday.

The Kurdish crackdown came a week after al-Zaidi ordered the army to prepare to enter Jurf al-Sakha r, south of Baghdad, where the government accuses the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah of running a smuggling operation.

Al Jazeera’s Mahmoud Abdelwahed, reporting from Erbil, said residents fear for their livelihoods if Baghdad takes over the region’s oil infrastructure, and spoke of a “trust deficiency” between the two governments. He said the Kurdish government denies any illicit oil operations and calls the campaign an attempt to undermine Kurdish constitutional and territorial rights.

A meeting sponsored by the head of the Supreme Judicial Council is set for December 1 in Baghdad, he said. If it fails or stalls, the sides could face a constitutional and political conflict.

Sajad Jiyad, an analyst at the Center for International Policy, told AFP that al-Zaidi’s “strategy is aligned with what America wants for Iraq and for its Iran policy”. Cutting off the oil flow, he said, is “exactly what US policy is right now: maximum pressure through economic blockade”.

Trump has welcomed al-Zaidi at the White House, where he called him “a great fighter” and “a great fan of America”.

articles.title: 'Privileged strategic partnership': Russian FM Lavrov hails ties with India
articles.summary: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has described India's ties with Moscow as a \"privileged strategic partnership\", highlighting the country's
articles.body: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has described India's ties with Moscow as a "privileged strategic partnership", highlighting the country's importance alongside China and Iran as Russia looks to strengthen its international partnerships amid a shift towards a multipolar world order.Speaking at a meeting with participants of the Alexander Gorchakov Public Diplomacy Fund's Dialogue for the Future programme in Moscow on Thursday, Lavrov said Russia continued to have strong partners despite deteriorating relations with Western countries."Our relations with India are officially described as a privileged strategic partnership. We also enjoy an especially advanced strategic partnership with the Islamic Republic of Iran, formalised in a treaty signed a year and a half ago," he said, as quoted by ANI.Referring to ties with Beijing, Lavrov said the Russia-China partnership had demonstrated its effectiveness at the recently concluded Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, including through the first-ever trilateral summit involving Russia, China and the United States.He also pointed to Russia's wider network of partnerships through groupings such as BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and the Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO)."We have no shortage of partners with whom to work," Lavrov said, describing BRICS as a "broad-based association of truly global reach".His remarks come amid continued diplomatic engagement between India and Russia over bilateral ties as well as the Ukraine conflict. Earlier this month, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said India had held discussions with Russia, Ukraine and European countries on three key issues arising from the war: protecting civilian shipping and seafarers, restoring grain exports through the Black Sea and preventing attacks on energy infrastructure.Speaking on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar said India was attempting to bring the concerned parties together to find common ground on these issues.He stressed that civilian vessels and seafarers should not be targeted and called for restoring grain shipments from both Russia and Ukraine, warning that exports through the Black Sea had declined sharply.On energy infrastructure, Jaishankar said reaching an understanding would be particularly complicated because countries had different interpretations of what needed protection, ranging from refineries and electricity grids to ships carrying fuel.Meanwhile, Lavrov also talked about Moscow's strategic relationship with Tehran. Russia and Iran signed a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in January 2025, covering cooperation in areas including trade, energy, science, technology and defence. The agreement entered into force in October that year.Making a broader assessment of global power dynamics, Lavrov said the traditional Western-dominated world order was giving way to new centres of economic and political influence."It is obvious to everyone that the issue concerns the tectonic shifts that are underway on the international stage, where the old world order, which was maintained for 500 years, first by Europeans and subsequently by the 'collective West,' is being replaced with new growth centres," he said.Describing multipolarity as an inevitable historical process, Lavrov argued that countries attempting to delay the transition would eventually have to engage with emerging centres of influence."Those who are trying to slow down this process can possibly hinder the rise of the new multipolar world order, but this will eventually take place anyway, and they will have to find common ground," he said.Taking aim at Western countries, he added that the United States, Europe and their allies could no longer dictate how other nations should conduct their international relations or decide whom they should cooperate with.Lavrov said Russia would continue to work through multilateral platforms, including the United Nations and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), while implementing decisions reached collectively.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Black Friday shoppers head to brick-and-mortar stores across the U.S.
articles.summary: The tradition of Black Friday bargain-hunting was alive and well this year as shoppers headed to malls around the country to scrounge for deals and revive an annual retail custom.
articles.body: The tradition of Black Friday bargain-hunting was alive and well this year as shoppers headed to malls around the country to scrounge for deals and revive an annual retail custom. Americans from coast to coast committed to the pre-Amazon memory of Thanksgiving weekend shopping, which lost steam in recent years as companies leaned into weekslong online sales and fewer early-morning doorbusters. “We’re happy to see people back in the mall,” Arly Klein of Teaneck, New Jersey, told NBC News on Friday at the Westfield Garden State Plaza mall, where she looked for holiday presents for family, friends and co-workers. “I feel like there were years, especially after Covid, where people weren’t really shopping in the stores,” Klein said. “We’re happy to, like, touch and feel and really like get the sense and feel the energy.” Simeon Siegel, a consumer equity researcher at Guggenheim Securities, was at the Paramus, New Jersey, retail hub observing the Black Friday scene. It “feels like what Black Friday used to feel like” down to to the shortage of mall parking, the industry expert said. “It’s fun again,” Siegel said. “People are coming to the mall not just because they feel like they need to — they feel like they want to.” The analyst said lines, early sales and crowds are still part of the Black Friday routine but “stampedes” and other extreme aspects of the yearly ordeal seem to be phasing out. The Citadel Outlets mall near Los Angeles was stirring with shoppers starting Thursday night, with lines forming around lit-up Christmas and palm trees outside storefronts, according to NBC Los Angeles. There was a similar scene at the Dolphin Mall in Miami, where punctual customers were rewarded with a mystery gift card with prizes ranging from $10 to $500, NBC South Florida reported. More shoppers were expected to to go to a physical store over the holiday weekend than at any point since 2019, according to a survey conducted by the ICSC, a commerce industry organization. The association also reported that more than 75% of participants in Thanksgiving weekend shopping also planned to dine out and that more than 50% were expected to splurge on entertainment and activities. Nearly 90% of adults in the U.S. planned to spend money over the holiday weekend, according to the survey. At a Boston-area shopping center, two women from England were on their 15th visit to the area for Thanksgiving and Black Friday. “We love the bargains that we can get here,” Sue Holloway told NBC Boston from the South Shore Plaza in Braintree, Massachusetts. “We can’t get them at home.” Holloway added that she and her traveling partner, Claire Caddy, “love to have a nice meal in the hotel and then we just shop, shop, shop.” Caddy said shopping in person is far better than the online alternative. “We like to come and see what we’re getting and choose for our family and friends,” Caddy said. “It’s not the same online.” Molly Zocco, of Newington, Connecticut, was at the Westfarms Mall early on Friday to keep a family tradition going. Other early discount-seekers also said they were drawn to the shopping center because it was a cherished ritual. “It’s definitely fun waking up early and going with my mom,” Zocco told NBC Connecticut.

articles.title: ‘Bear trap’: Ukraine hails new operation as Russian casualties mount
articles.summary: Russian assaults met with stout defence along the front as Western powers discuss ceasefire proposals.
articles.body:
Ukraine’s forces liberated more of their land as Russia broke new casualty records and United States negotiators tried to convince Kyiv to give up territory, or NATO membership.

Details emerged on November 20 of a new operation – the fourth this year – in which Ukraine said it cleared Russian troops out of hundreds of square kilometres of land they occupied, this time in the northern Kharkiv region.

That was about a month after Russia said it had encircled 2,000 Ukrainian troops in an enclave adjacent to the Russian border, around the town of Velykyi Burluk.

Ukrainian commanders realised that the troops were in danger of being encircled, and ordered the execution of “Operation Bear Trap”, which relied on deceptive moves and secrecy to attack the enemy from various sides, concealing its main direction.

Ukrainian forces used a Russian T-80 tank and an Abrams M-1 tank to attack the border town of Vilhuvatka, giving the impression that their main blow would land there.

They then attacked Russian reinforcements from the rear as they arrived to shore up defences, and used drones to remotely mine Russian resupply routes.

The Ukrainian command said Operation Bear Trap has so far succeeded in liberating 200sq km (77sq miles) and 14 settlements, and was ongoing.

Russian troops continue to occupy at least four border villages in Kharkiv, including Vovchansk, but their plan to seize almost 500sq km (193sq miles) has been foiled.

It is not the first time Ukrainian forces preempted a Russian pincer movement.

Earlier this year they stopped an attempted encirclement of the “fortress belt” of Sloviansk, Kramatorsk and Druzhivka in the eastern Donetsk region during Operation Vivaldi .

But Kyiv still struggled to defend its skies and nationwide power outages are making life miserable for Ukrainians.

Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces in Donetsk were engaged in active defence, stopping attempted assaults and destroying vehicles.

Retired Ukrainian colonel Konstantyn Mashovets, who analyses the front on his Telegram channel, said Kyiv’s forces had also advanced in southern Zaporizhia, clearing Russian infiltrators out of the northern bank of the Solona river near Novopavlivka.

As Russia continued these assaults, its casualties rose to a record on November 24 of 432,519, Ukraine’s military said. The next day, it set a new monthly record of 55,629 for November, with five days to go in the month.

Despite Ukraine’s battlefield achievements, US mediation offers remained unchanged.

US negotiators had put two proposals before Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported, citing people involved in talks. Both involved an exchange of land for peace.

In one, Ukraine would cede the “fortress belt” of cities in Donetsk and receive full NATO membership, the WSJ said.

But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected the idea of retreating from that well-defended position.

Russian official Dmitry Medvedev reiterated on November 20 that Ukraine’s potential NATO membership was a key reason for the war. He also suggested partitioning Ukraine, proposing that Lviv could be handed to Poland as part of a deal.

“The enemy has not abandoned its goal of destroying Ukrainian statehood,” said Ukraine’s Defence Ministry.

US negotiator Jared Kushner told a Berlin news conference that Russia had accepted a watered-down version of this US proposal – the second option outlined by the WSJ – of creating NATO-style security guarantees for Ukraine in return for freezing the front line.

“We have been able to convince the Russians of this concept that any security guarantees for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” Kushner said. “President Trump is open to it, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest.”

It would be in the US interest, as he explained on social media, if “broader security arrangements made it highly unlikely that the guarantee would ever be invoked. This is why security guarantees for Ukraine cannot be finalised in isolation from post-war European security architecture.”

It appeared, therefore, that Europe would have to assume the burden of a future defence of Ukraine, something Russia has also rejected, because it refuses to accept European forces on Ukrainian soil.

Those NATO-style guarantees would have to be offered from the safety of NATO soil, rendering them less effective.

Zelenskyy told journalists he did not trust a deal between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom Trump referred to as “my friend” on November 19.

He told Bloomberg the US and Russia were effectively in cahoots to bully Ukraine.

“It’s very unfortunate when, during discussions about how to end the war, Starshield either malfunctions or has limitations , and not only are there fewer missiles for Patriot systems, but there are also other issues that prevent deliveries,” he said.

“Politically, it looks as if [the US] is moving in the same direction as what Putin wants: to force Ukraine into unfavourable compromises,” Zelenskyy said.

Europe did not appear to be in a listening mood any more than Ukraine.

“Russia wants more than Ukraine,” German chancellor Friedrich Merz told parliament. “Russia is escalating in the Baltic. Russia is escalating in Poland. Russia is escalating on the Black Sea. Russia is escalating in space, and Russia is escalating massively here in our own country.”

Merz was referring to two Russian missiles and a Russian drone, which crashed in an area of Poland on November 20, where a multinational force of more than 5,000 personnel from Britain, France, Belgium, Estonia, Spain, the Netherlands, Lithuania, Germany, Poland and Sweden was conducting its first military exercise.

Ukraine made its own response to Russia very clear during the past week.

On November 21 it struck the Sparta II , a Russian logistics vessel en route from St. Petersburg to Kaliningrad.

The next day two Ukrainian naval drones struck and sank the Russian corvette Merkury near the Libyan port of Benghazi, in an attack that has caused tensions between Italy and Ukraine .

“The operation involved 7 unmanned boats manufactured in Ukraine, which were transported to the designated location and launched from a ‘mother ship’,” said the Ukraine Security Force (SBU).

On the same day, Ukraine struck another Russian logistics ship, the Angara, also in the Mediterranean.

Ukraine’s strikes inside Russia also continued.

On November 25, Ukrainian forces attacked the Savasleyka airfield, damaging a Mig-31 and two Sukhoi-24 bombers, all used to launch Khinzal missiles. Three days earlier, Russia had fired 84 cruise missiles into Ukraine.

Ukraine struck the Kaleykino pumping station, which sits on the Druzhba oil pipeline and helps export Russian crude, on November 20 and again on November 23. The strikes reportedly destroyed three 50,000 tonne oil tanks.

During the week Ukraine also struck the Novoshakhtinsk, Permnefteorgsintez, Kuibishevsk, and Sizran refineries, all key to supplying the Russian military. The furthest of these was 3,000km (1,800 miles) from unoccupied Ukraine.

Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries have lowered its refining capacity by an estimated one-third, and caused fuel shortages .

Ukraine’s military intelligence estimated that over the three months ending on October 22, Russia imported almost a million tonnes of refined fuels, including 128,000 tonnes of diesel.

articles.title: In 1947, architect John Lautner designed a Hollywood Hills home with a roof supported by a three-point steel structure; the preserved two-bedroom Polin House is now listed for $2.85 million
articles.summary: A preserved two-bedroom house designed by architect John Lautner in 1947 has been listed for sale in the Hollywood Hills for $2,850,000.
articles.body: A preserved two-bedroom house designed by architect John Lautner in 1947 has been listed for sale in the Hollywood Hills for $2,850,000. The property gives buyers a rare chance to own one of his early designs, which explored new ways of supporting a building. Known as the Florence Polin House, it measures 1,342 square feet and stands at 3542 Multiview Drive, above the Cahuenga Pass. It sits on a hillside plot covering more than half an acre. One of the home's most unusual features is the way its roof is supported. A three-point steel truss carries the weight, so the inside walls do not need to support the roof. This leaves the living areas open and allows rooms to be arranged more freely. According to LA Digs, the property is listed by Mortimer Canepa of Berkshire Hathaway and Nicole Kornhauser of Carolwood Estates. Nearly eight decades after it was built, the house still retains much of its original mid-century style.How the steel roof shapes the layoutLautner designed the Polin House for Florence Polin in 1947. It was an early project in his career in Southern California, after he had spent six years working with Frank Lloyd Wright. Property details on Debbie Pisaro's architectural website list 1948 as the year the house was built, while giving 1947 as the year Lautner designed it. Rather than using regular walls inside the house to support the roof, Lautner created a three-point steel structure to carry its weight. Architecture blog Architectoid explains that placing the supports towards the outside frees up the floor space below. This allows rooms to flow into one another without large internal walls blocking views or movement. According to Debbie Pisaro's architectural report, the Polin House is one of three homes Lautner designed using a steel truss to support the roof. It is also next to his 1947 Jacobsen House on Multiview Drive, which follows a closely related design.Living spaces and canyon viewsInside the 1,342-square-foot house, Lautner used low, horizontal lines and large glass walls to connect the home with the steep hillside around it. LA Digs reports that the property has two bedrooms and two bathrooms and stands on a plot measuring about 26,612 square feet. A large brick fireplace stretches from floor to ceiling in the open-plan living room. It also works as a partial divider between areas of the room, LA Digs reported. Dark wooden panelled ceilings, exposed structural beams and concrete floors give the space a simple, solid feel that suits its hillside setting. Angled glass walls run around the outside of the house and frame views across the canyon. The dining area is set in a narrow section lined with glass, with exposed wooden framing and a sloping timber ceiling. Sliding glass doors open onto the garden on one side, while a long brick wall runs along the other, LA Digs noted.Terraces and indoor outdoor flowOutdoor areas are an important part of the home's design and everyday use. LA Digs reported that glass walls open onto terraces that wrap around the house, along with partly enclosed sunrooms. These spaces allow residents to eat outdoors while remaining sheltered from the weather. The house has a low, horizontal shape and rests on concrete supports. Rows of windows sit beneath a shallow roof, showing Lautner's early interest in building around the shape of a steep hillside instead of flattening the land. Concrete, steel framing and wooden cladding remain visible both inside and outside the property.Market history and current listingWith an asking price of $2,850,000, the house is being offered at about $2,124 per square foot, according to real estate figures collected on Debbie Pisaro's architectural website. This is roughly 1.9 times the $1,495,000 asking price reported in a 2011 Los Angeles Times feature. John Lautner's homes rarely come up for sale on the open market in Los Angeles, and many owners keep them for years. For buyers interested in his early work in the Hollywood Hills, the listing at 3542 Multiview Drive brings a preserved 1947 design, built around an unusual steel roof structure, back onto the market.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Kyiv offers Black Sea ceasefire to protect grain exports
articles.summary: The proposal comes as President Zelenskyy criticises Trump’s ‘friendship’ with Putin.
articles.body:
Ukraine has presented a proposal for a possible ceasefire in the Black Sea, as Kyiv seeks to protect its grain exports amid escalating attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.

Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced the proposal on Friday during the “Food from Ukraine” conference, saying Kyiv was ready to restore freedom of navigation and ensure the uninterrupted export of agricultural products.

“We are now awaiting a response from Russia. All of our proposals have been conveyed,” Sybiha said.

Moscow has sought to include oil transportation in the proposed ceasefire deal, but the Ukrainians say that issue belongs in a broader energy ceasefire.

He accused Russia of repeatedly putting forward “unrealistic demands” in response to Kyiv’s proposals, according to Suspilne, Ukraine’s national broadcaster.

The latest ceasefire initiative comes amid growing international concern over the security of commercial shipping and global food supplies. Ukraine and Russia are both major agricultural exporters , and attacks on vessels and port infrastructure have disrupted shipments transiting through the Black Sea.

A previous UN- and Turkiye-brokered agreement allowed Ukrainian grain exports to resume following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.

However, Moscow withdrew from the arrangement in July 2023, prompting Kyiv to establish an alternative maritime export corridor.

In August, Reuters reported that Ukraine had conveyed an earlier proposal through a third party for both sides to halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea. At the time, Ukrainian grain exports had fallen 76 percent year-on-year, as shipowners avoided ports in the Odesa region following repeated Russian strikes.

International efforts to secure a limited ceasefire have since gained traction.

On October 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was reviewing proposals from Turkiye and India to facilitate uninterrupted grain and energy shipments.

The diplomatic impasse also comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy voiced his frustrations with US President Donald Trump’s approach to Moscow.

In an interview with the BBC on Friday, Zelenskyy criticised Trump for describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” following their meeting in China last week.

“It’s strange. He is an aggressor and a killer. He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be,” Zelenskyy said.

He also criticised Washington for what he described as excessive neutrality in its dealings with Moscow, arguing that the US should use its influence to pressure Russia into meaningful negotiations.

“When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor … it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It’s not right,” he said.

After talks in Florida on Wednesday, the NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called on Russia to avoid actions that could expand the war and urged a peaceful resolution as soon as possible.

Rutte has also stressed that any eventual peace agreement or long-term ceasefire must include security guarantees for Ukraine.

articles.title: Mexico files complaint with US over DEA tip line on alleged drug dealers
articles.summary: Tensions rise over DEA tip line, with Mexico emphasising respect for its sovereignty amidst growing bilateral discord.
articles.body:
Mexico has filed a formal complaint with the ⁠United States over a US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) tip line seeking information on suspected drug traffickers and alleged corruption among Mexican officials , President Claudia Sheinbaum has announced, touching on a particularly sensitive issue in bilateral relations.

Foreign Minister Juan Ramon ⁠de la Fuente contacted the US ambassador to Mexico to lodge the complaint, Sheinbaum said on Friday during her morning news conference, adding that the ambassador said he would look into the issue.

Alleged links between elected officials and organised crime have become an increasingly fraught issue for Sheinbaum’s government, which has rejected what it describes as attempts by US authorities to interfere in Mexican ‌affairs.

“We have made it very clear that our relationship with the United States is one of coordination, not subordination,” Sheinbaum said.

The complaint comes despite a significant expansion of security cooperation between the two nations under Sheinbaum. Her government has stepped up efforts against organised crime and fentanyl trafficking amid pressure from US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly threatened unilateral action against Mexican cartels if Mexico did not do more.

On Thursday, Sheinbaum in harsh comments Thursday, read excerpts from a new investigation by The Associated Press news agency revealing how the DEA allowed at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills to go unseized as it spent eight months tracking a drug trafficking ring flooding the southwestern US with deadly drugs.

“The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot,” Sheinbaum said. “The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organised crime, or what they call terrorist groups.”

Recent cooperation has included the capture of drug lord Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “ El Chapo Isidro “, in an operation Mexican officials said was carried out by ⁠Mexican troops supported by US intelligence.

Bilateral security cooperation, however, has been ⁠repeatedly tested. The DEA has long been a source of friction, with Mexican officials accusing the agency of overstepping its authority and infringing on national sovereignty.

Tensions also flared earlier this year after two US officials who were killed in the northern state of Chihuahua were identified by sources ⁠as CIA personnel, exposing US intelligence activities that Sheinbaum said her government was not aware of.

The DEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment by the Reuters news agency on the Mexican complaint.

The ⁠US agency this week announced a tip line seeking information on alleged ⁠members of criminal organisations, corrupt officials and others collaborating with drug traffickers in Sinaloa, the northwestern Mexican state that is the stronghold of the Sinaloa Cartel.

“Your information matters. Your identity and your safety matter,” DEA Administrator Terry Cole said in a post on social media, specifying that tips submitted via Signal, WhatsApp and email would be handled confidentially.

The tip line comes amid broader US pressure on Mexico over suspected links between politicians and cartels.

Reuters reported in June that the Trump administration ‌had pressed Mexico to investigate politicians suspected of cartel links and extradite them to the US to face criminal charges. Those discussions included allegations involving figures from Sheinbaum’s governing Morena party, according to sources familiar with the talks.

Among the politicians ‌who ‌have faced US scrutiny is Sinaloa Governor Ruben Rocha Moya, who has repeatedly denied wrongdoing.

Sheinbaum added on Friday that “the United States should focus on tackling drug consumption and criminal groups operating within its own territory.”

articles.title: NHS Grampian publishes leaked report at centre of hospital scandal
articles.summary: The report was leaked last week by a surgeon who called for NHS Grampian to face a corporate homicide investigation.
articles.body:
NHS Grampian has published the internal report which revealed there had been 19 avoidable deaths of patients who had undergone liver and pancreatic surgery at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.

It was leaked last week by surgeon Dr Mohammed Habib, who called for NHS Grampian to face a corporate homicide probe after the report said some patients bled to death on the operating table.

NHS Grampian has now released the report from September 2022, along with a redacted version of a follow-up from November the same year.

The health board said they were being published now "in the interests of absolute transparency".

Meanwhile, written submissions have also been published from witnesses who will appear at the Scottish Parliament's health committee next week.

These include two whistleblowers and Prof Caroline Hiscox, former chief executive NHS Grampian.

Separately, the health board has apologised after confidential papers containing sensitive medical and personal details of 22 patients were found discarded on a street near Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.

A passer-by found the documents near a bin on Raeden Park Road, near Foresterhill Health Campus, on Thursday.

NHS Grampian has been at the centre of controversy since a report from the health watchdog published two weeks ago highlighted "major deficiencies" in its leadership and culture.

NHS Grampian scandal should be watershed moment - BMA

'My wife would still be alive if NHS Grampian had followed medical guidelines'

NHS Grampian surgeon was ready to operate while recovering from medical procedure

Habib, a consultant surgeon at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary (ARI), leaked the 2022 report the following week.

The Scottish government then announced an independent review into concerns around hepatobiliary (HPB) surgery at the health board.

A number of patients have come forward to raise concerns about their treatment.

On Thursday, Scotland's chief medical officer Sir Gregor Smith, who had faced questions over his role, resigned on mental health grounds.

The September 2022 report was written by Prof Stephen Wigmore, regius professor of clinical surgery at Edinburgh University.

It looked at 45 patients in the care of liver and pancreatic services at ARI between 2015 and 2021.

It said 31 had died, and 19 of them were considered to have died of avoidable consequences of surgery or intervention.

The review criticised decision-making in liver surgery for occasionally being "overly aggressive", with surgery going ahead even if the disease was thought to be inoperable.

In pancreatic surgery, patients were regularly rushed into theatre without adequate planning or consideration of non-surgical alternatives, the report said.

A follow-up report was published in November 2022 where Wigmore was asked to review more HPB surgery cases which had not been within the scope of his original report.

It found unacceptably high mortality rates for some pancreatic surgeries, as well as "extremely high" blood loss for a number of pancreas and liver operations.

The professor said surgeons had low caseloads, which harmed their technical experience.

He offered to support the surgeons, then issued a letter in May 2023 which said HPB services at NHS Grampian had improved and was now safe.

The health board's chief executive Laura Skaife-Knight said the names of patients and families had been redacted from the second report to protect their identities, and the health board was "contacting/re-engaging" them to offer support.

"I recognise the significant concern the events of the last week have caused our patients and local community," she said.

"However, I would encourage anyone who needs our care to come forward at the earliest opportunity.

"Please continue to engage with our healthcare services and attend appointments and operations as normal. Our priority remains patient safety."

Prof Hiscox, who was in charge of NHS Grampian when the reports were written, has submitted evidence ahead of the Holyrood health committee meeting on Wednesday.

She said the NHS Grampian board was fully briefed on the first Wigmore report at a meeting on 27 October 2022.

This was done to "protect patient and staff confidentiality", provide time for patients and families to be contacted, and "enable full and frank discussion of the issues and avoid causing undue public alarm that could potentially increase the likelihood of late presentation and possibly lead to poorer health outcomes".

Her evidence said this "communications approach was shared with relevant officials at Scottish government".

She also said the families of 17 of the 19 patients whose deaths had been avoidable were contacted, but contact details could not be identified for the other two.

A Scottish government spokesperson said the documents released to date had shown that a number of government officials were aware of the concerns raised by Dr Habib.

"It is a matter of public record that the Scottish government has engaged on the concerns raised by Dr Habib over a number of years," it said.

The spokesperson added that the independent review would deliver "clarity, transparency and accountability to patients and their families".

Did Scotland's departing chief medical officer actually do anything wrong?

A question of trust in the NHS could be Swinney's most dangerous political moment

Does Scotland's NHS have a revolving door problem with senior managers?

The committee will also hear from two whistleblowers who have raised concerns about patient safety at NHS Grampian.

In his evidence ahead of the hearing, Dr Izhar Khan - who currently works as a consultant pephrologist at ARI - said the roots of the problems dated back more than 14 years.

"For years senior management has not listened to clinical advice and on occasions when advice was given, often it was ignored," he said.

The senior clinician also said he believed Dr Gray's Hospital in Elgin, Moray, was not fit for purpose to deliver acute services.

Dr Khan said the health board needed "strong and resilient leadership that listens to clinicians and staff".

Prof Zygmunt Krukowski, former consultant general surgeon at ARI, has also written to the committee ahead of his appearance.

He said it was "distressing" to see the reputation of the hospital where he worked for more than 40 years damaged by "inept management and clinical governance".

"If there had been effective clinical leadership and management the pattern of poor care which was clinically obvious as early as 2010 would have been addressed," he added.

The confidential papers found discarded on a street on Thursday are believed to consist of four crumpled pages, dated from the day before.

They are understood to have listed names, CHI numbers and medical conditions of 22 neurosurgery patients.

NHS Grampian's senior information risk officer, Shantini Paranjothy said: "We are making efforts to contact those patients whose data was contained in these documents and apologise for the distress this has caused.

"Investigations into how these documents ended up in a public place are under way and this incident has been reported to the Information Commissioner's Office.

"Patients have the right to expect their data to be stored securely. We take the issue of data protection very seriously."

articles.title: Road or straight line? Different distance rules leave parents guessing the yardstick
articles.summary: Delhi nursery admissions: Schools use varying distance methods—aerial, road, transport links, colony lists or GIS—causing inconsistent proximity scores for parents.
articles.body: New Delhi: For parents applying to private schools in Delhi for nursery admissions, measuring the distance between home and school should be simple. But it isn’t. The same address can earn a child different distance scores at different schools, depending on how each one calculates proximity.With neighbourhood distance carrying significant weight in nursery admissions, the lack of a uniform method has left parents doing more than just filling forms. They must also figure out how each school measures the distance before knowing how many points their child could get.“I have been closely following the admission process as my son is due to start school in the next academic session. While the points-based system looks good on paper, calculating the distance for each school is a task in itself. The problem is that I may calculate the distance using one method, while the school may use an entirely different one to verify it. This means I have to check with every school about the method it follows and then make separate calculations to see whether we qualify,” said Deepali Raina, a mother.One of the methods being used by schools is aerial or straight-line distance, which measures the shortest geographical distance between a child’s home and the school, ignoring roads, traffic and barriers such as rivers, railway lines and highways. Two homes that appear equally close on a map may therefore have very different road distances. This method measures geographical proximity, not the distance a child would actually travel. Some others use road distance, calculating the route between the home and school through the road network.“While seeking admission for my child, I found that schools followed different methods to calculate distance. What confused me was that I qualified for a certain number of distance points at one school but not at another located right next to it. Although both schools were almost equally accessible from my home, their distance calculations produced different results,” said Prateek Kapoor, another parent.Some schools factor in transport connectivity rather than geographical distance, calculating proximity through bus routes, designated stops or access to their transport network. This could mean a child living closer to a school but without a direct transport link scores fewer points than one living farther away but better connected. Others follow a colony-wise or neighbourhood-based system, awarding points based on lists of residential areas rather than individual addresses.Schools may also use a radius-based system, placing applicants in distance brackets of 3 km, 5 km, 10 km or 15 km. However, the score can vary depending on whether the distance is measured in a straight line or along roads. articles.title: Parsvnath directors denied bail as consumer commission flags evasion of proceedings
articles.summary: State consumer commission denied bail to Parsvnath Developers directors for evading execution proceedings; noted pending homebuyer cases and arrests in Nov 2026.
articles.body: New Delhi: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has rejected pleas by Parsvnath Developers Ltd directors Sanjeev Kumar Jain and Rajeev Jain seeking recall of earlier orders and release on bail. The commission pulled them up for repeatedly evading execution proceedings despite being represented by lawyers at every hearing.It held that subsequent settlements with homebuyers and payment undertakings could not erase their past conduct or allay concerns that they might evade the judicial process again if released.The commission, presided over by Justice Sangita Dhingra Sehgal and member Bimla Kumari, noted that the directors were represented by advocates at every hearing. Their lawyers took instructions on outstanding payments but failed to produce them despite specific directions.“The counsels for the applicants were fully aware of the proceedings, yet the applicants chose to disregard the mandate of this commission,” it observed, adding that the directors were “observing the proceedings behind the curtain”.More than 100 execution matters were pending against Parsvnath Developers and its group entities, including Parsvnath Buildwell Pvt Ltd. Of the 79 petitions tracked, 65 remained pending and 14 had been settled, the order stated.The commission said the directors’ continued absence was neither “isolated nor inadvertent”. Police could not trace them at their recorded addresses.After the warrants remained unexecuted, the commission initiated proclaimed offender proceedings, with notices published in The Hindu and Jansatta in Feb 2026. Crime Branch eventually tracked and arrested the directors near 11 Murti on Nov 2. They were produced before the commission the next day.Rejecting their plea for release to facilitate settlements with homebuyers, the commission noted that they had settled 17 of 47 pending execution matters while in custody.“The contention that their release is indispensable for facilitating settlements with the remaining decree holders does not inspire confidence,” it said, noting that they could negotiate settlements and arrange payments even from custody.The commission held that subsequent settlements, payment proposals and undertakings could not “efface their previous conduct” or allay fears that they might evade the judicial process if released.Earlier, Justice Sehgal had remanded the directors to judicial custody until Nov 18 in over 40 execution cases involving unpaid homebuyer refunds and compensation.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.summary: TNA star KC Navarro overcame school bullying and a knee injury on his road to the Ultimate X win, and now he opens up to kids in El Paso, Texas.
articles.body: Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA) star KC Navarro has been through the wringer as he tries to capture his first championship in the company, including a significant knee injury and a few missed opportunities. When he was younger, he also had to go through bullying at school as he tried to stay on track to achieve his dream of becoming a professional wrestler. articles.title: Powerful Thanksgiving Day storm causes flooding, power outages
articles.summary: The storm hammered sections of the East Coast with torrential rain, high winds and flooding, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of customers.
articles.body:
A Thanksgiving storm brought foul weather to the East Coast and Midwest on Thursday, causing major power outages , disrupting holiday travel and prompting the historic postponement of New York City's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

More than 500,000 customers were without power Friday afternoon across the Midwest and Northeast, according to the utility tracking website PowerOutage.us . Of those, more than 122,000 customers were without electricity in Pennsylvania, along with more than 92,000 in New Jersey and 66,000 in Maryland. The outages reached more than 800,000 customers at the height of the storm Thursday night.

There were 1,673 flights in the U.S. delayed as of Friday midday, with another 119 canceled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware . But that is a far cry from the more than 2,500 flights to or from U.S. destinations delayed on Thursday, while more than 460 were canceled, according to FlightAware.

The storm hammered sections of the East Coast with torrential rain, high winds and flooding. All of New Jersey was under a state of emergency , declared by Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Wednesday night, as were parts of New York , following a declaration from Gov. Kathy Hochul. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic to southern New England.

Stormy weather creates havoc in New York City

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday morning that two people had to be rescued from their cars because of flooding. He cautioned people not to attempt to walk, bike or drive through flooded areas.

"We want to remind everyone to stay safe and there is no destination worth your safety," Mamdani said.

The New York City Emergency Management agency reported that the city received 1.5 to 2 inches of rain on Thanksgiving, with some parts seeing up to 3 inches. High tides brought flooding to the city's coastal areas, including portions of Staten Island and Long Island.

Central Park saw wind gusts higher than 30 mph, the agency said, while LaGuardia Airport recorded winds of 56 mph. Several scaffolding structures collapsed in the wind, with no injuries were reported.

Macy's postponed the annual Thanksgiving parade until Saturday because of concerns about how the parade's massive balloons would fare in the wind-swept canyons between Manhattan's skyscrapers.

A high school marching band from Pearland, Texas, near Houston, said it raised a staggering $350,000 to allow its 500 members to stay in New York City for two extra nights.

"This was quite a challenge for us, and there was a very frantic and large call to action to our community to let the kids stay here and finish it out," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band for Pearland High School, told CBS News on Thursday.

Visitors who had traveled to New York to attend the parade were forced to make last-minute changes to their travel plans. Amanda Anderson, a Florida-based makeup artist who was hired to do makeup for parade performers, told CBS News New York she was able to rebook her flights so she could stay an extra day.

"I was in Macy's, actually, when I found out, and I look up and there was like three girls crying already," Anderson said when she learned the parade had been postponed. "People were sitting down, very somber. It was an experience."

Major roadways flooded, holiday travel disrupted

The storm flooded coastal villages and cities from North Carolina through New Jersey as the high tide rolled in Thursday morning. Roads were closed and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water.

Avalon, New Jersey, was seeing some of the worst flooding in its history, Borough of Avalon Business Administrator Scott J. Wahl said.

"Not quite Hurricane Sandy," Wahl said of the benchmark storm for his village on the far south of New Jersey's Atlantic coast.

Floodwaters washed debris over the road next to the shore, and a few drivers had to be rescued after driving around barricades and into floodwaters, but no injuries were reported, Wahl said.

Lance Miller, 54, said floods in his neighborhood of Ocean City, a small coastal town in New Jersey, are about a foot deep and that driving to the nearest grocery store would probably "destroy your car."

"I wouldn't do that, I'm a car guy," said Miller. "You're gonna have a good foot of water that you'd have to drive through."

Miller, who had his Thanksgiving Day meal preparations set, said he would be staying indoors and have dinner with his wife and daughter. But he said some of his friends in the area were "not so lucky" and had flooding inside their homes.

"So they're dealing with cleanup, you know," he said.

The Margate City Fire Department near Atlantic City, New Jersey, posted a video on Facebook of water pouring through the city's streets on a gray day even before heavy rains started.

A firefighter there said the tide was coming in ferociously and it was still an hour before its peak. Water closed in on steps to houses, and businesses had sandbags piled in front of their doors.

A stretch of U.S. Route 30, a major artery that goes into Atlantic City, was shuttered in both directions due to heavy flooding, the Absecon Police Department reported.

"Please stay off the roads until conditions improve," Absecon police said. "Do not attempt to drive through flooded roadways or around barricades."

Chester County Hospital in West Chester, Pennsylvania, sustained a partial power outage on Thursday afternoon, but power was restored before patients had to be transported to other facilities.

Residents of the Pennsylvania community of Springfield Township north of Philadelphia were asked to temporarily evacuate out of caution after a tree fell on a propane tank, local officials said. That evacuation advisory was later lifted.

The storm prompted the temporary closure of some coastal highways and bridges. The nearly 18-mile Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel over the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia was closed for several hours Thursday morning because of high winds, while NC 12, the only highway connecting Hatteras Island on the North Carolina Outer Banks to the mainland, was closed after seawater breached the dunes again and covered the two-lane highway.

North Carolina was particularly hard-hit by heavy rain. Emerald Isle, in the state's Outer Banks, received 9.16 inches of rain. Atlantic Beach, North Carolina, saw 9.06 inches.

In Maryland, nearly 2 million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George's counties, which are in the Washington metropolitan area, were asked to conserve water by the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission because of intermittent power disruptions associated with the storm. The water conservation request, which applied to all 1.9 million WSSC customers, was due to the risk that power outages posed to the agency's two water filtration plants.

Heavy snow fell on parts of Illinois and Missouri with St. Louis recording 7.3 inches of snowfall. French Village, Missouri, received 15 inches of show while Ste. Genevieve recorded 14 inches.

The ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, which hosts hockey and other ice skating activities, was empty when the roof caved in at about 3 a.m., according to the city.

The rain isn't quite over yet for the Northeast. More storms are expected Sunday night into Monday morning for New York City, Philadelphia and Boston.
